Topic: By-Elections

One Nation candidate David Farley (left) and party leader Pauline Hanson (right) celebrate victory in the Farrer by-election. ( AAP: Bianca de Marchi )

One Nation has scored a thumping win in the Farrer by-election, marking the first time the party has won a Lower House seat in federal parliament.

The ABC's election analyst Casey Briggs called the seat for One Nation just after 8:00pm.

At that stage One Nation candidate David Farley had more than 40 per cent of the primary vote and was predicted to win the seat with a margin of about nine per cent after preferences.

The result saw One Nation record not only a landslide but an historic victory in Farrer, as the Coalition lost part of its heartland and the jewel in its crown — a seat it had held for nearly 80 years.

Mr Farley said he chose to join One Nation because it was "a political party of courage and tenacity".

"I wanted to match that to what my skills were … in agriculture, agribusiness and community, and I could see the job that was required," he said.

"So I look at it and I understand what is the job in Farrer, what's got to be required and how to deliver it, and that message plus our policies has resonated very well right across the whole depth and breadth of Farrer.

Mr Farley said his victory meant the party was now "at the end of its beginning".

"We're like a mason with a chisel and a hammer, and we're re-carving the letters into the Australian democracy," he said.

One Nation Leader Pauline Hanson addressed a jubilant victory party, telling supporters "we're coming after those other seats".

"We are here to represent you, the people, and to get our country back," she said.

One Nation had never won a seat in the federal House of Representatives, although Barnaby Joyce now flies its colours in the lower house after defecting from the Nationals .

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson was elected in 1996 after being disendorsed by the Liberal Party for controversial remarks about Indigenous Australians, but that happened so late in the campaign that her name appeared on the ballot as a Liberal.

She subsequently lost her seat in 1998.

Voters in the Farrer by-election had the choice of 12 candidates. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn )

A dozen candidates contested the seat , which was held by the Coalition since its creation in 1949 and by former Liberal Party leader Sussan Ley for the last quarter of a century.

In the 2025 federal election the Liberal Party secured more than 43 per cent of first-preference votes.

Independent Michelle Milthorpe secured 20 per cent, with Labor on 15 per cent and One Nation just shy of seven.

A year later the by-election has delivered a dramatically different result.

The four-cornered contest saw both Coalition parties relegated to the status of also-rans.

With about 45 per cent of the vote counted, Liberal candidate Raissa Butkowski had 11.47 per cent of the vote and the Nationals Brad Robertson 9.59 per cent.

Their decision to preference One Nation ahead of the independent Ms Milthorpe has made her task vastly more difficult.

Ms Milthorpe has attracted about 25 per cent of the primary vote, but if Coalition voters follow their candidates' how-to-vote cards she will not be receiving their preferences.

She told her supporters the electorate would "never be taken for granted again".

"We are no longer satisfied with being a safe seat that gets very little attention or funding from the government of the day," Ms Milthorpe said.

"We see the political class as totally disconnected from our everyday lives, and we are more than ready than ever to register our disconnect at the ballot box."

Albury councillor Raissa Butkowski contested the Farrer by-election for the Liberals. ( ABC News: Greg Ryan )

The deputy leader of the Liberals, Jane Hume, would not be drawn on whether it was the correct decision.

"I'm not going to speculate on preferences, that really is a decision for the party organisation, not for the candidates and not for the politicians themselves," she said.

But Liberals leader Angus Taylor told the ABC it was the right move.

"I am very confident that's what out voters in this electorate wanted us to do, and it's what we did," he said.

Mr Taylor told party supporters the by-election was "always going to be a mountain to climb".

"We have to take away some hard lessons from this," he said.

"For too long we have been a party of convenience, not of conviction and that must change."

Mr Taylor said the party needed to "take our medicine and be honest with the Australian people".

"Mass migration has not worked for this country, 1.4 million people in three and a half years, it has not worked for this country," he said.

The Nationals deputy leader Bridget McKenzie told the ABC she would be open to the prospect of forming a minority government with One Nation in the future.

"I'd be willing to work with anyone that wants to see Anthonty Albanese leave the lodge," she said.

"I don't care what colour you are, I'm interested in delivering results and building a prosperous and healthy country."

Nationals leader Matt Canavan described the by-election as "a bit of a reintroduction for us for the people of Albury and southern NSW".

"But we are not going anywhere. We are here for the long haul," he said.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan became a familiar face in the electorate of Farrer during the lead up to the by-election. ( ABC News: Philippe Perez )

Former Liberal leader Sussan Ley, whose resignation sparked the by-election, released a statement statement expressing "immense disappointment about this loss".

"The seat of Farrer was created in 1949. Until tonight, at every one of the 30 elections since, through different and challenging circumstances, it has been held without exception by the Liberal and National parties," she said. "It would be an error to reduce both the scale and significance of tonight's defeat to a Coalition split which occurred months ago, or to misattribute it to the date the vote was held.

"I urge the Liberal leadership to accept this result with humility because the voters never get it wrong."

Ms Ley said on the day the leadership spilled in February, the new leader said the Liberal Party needed to "change or die".

"Three months later, the result in Farrer demonstrates that statement to be far truer today than it ever was then," she said.

Sussan ley's resignation sparked the Farrer by-election. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

One Nation's member for New England, former Nationals leader Barnaby Joyce, was quick to pour scorn on the Liberals' performance.

"The Libs got 11 per cent, honest to goodness ... it's like the Marijuana Party," he said.

Polling day had its share of controversy with the Federal Court issuing an injunction ordering the removal of signage claiming to be authorised by the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC).

The posters were spotted on a fence at the Orana Community Centre at Springdale Heights, north of Albury.

They depicted an AEC transparency register of political donations to independent candidate Ms Milthorpe who has been under fire from her opponents over contributions to her campaign from Climate 200.

In a statement the AEC said the signs had the potential to misrepresent the source of the corflute.

"While it includes information from the AEC's transparency register, the AEC did not erect or authorise the signage," it said.

It did not disclose who was responsible.

The Federal Court has granted an injunction for the unauthorised sign to be removed. ( Supplied: Australian Electoral Commission )

Conservative voters were spoilt for choice when it came to choosing a candidate, but all four aspiring MPs expressed similar views on what emerged as the key issue: water.

All went on the record as being opposed to further water buybacks in the Murray-Darling Basin and supporting further investigation of the basin's management.

The electorate of Farrer covers 126,563 square kilometres, or nearly 16 per cent of New South Wales. ( Supplied: Sussan Ley )

They also voiced support for more scrutiny and decreasing immigrant numbers — although this was a more delicate issue in an electorate with strong multicultural communities and local industries that rely on migrant workers.

Mr Farley will now have to find a way to work with the Albanese government if he is to deliver on the pledges made during the campaign.

Topic: World Politics

Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a speech during Victory Day celebrations in Red Square. ( Kremlin.ru via Reuters )

Russia has held a scaled-back Victory Day parade amid deepening concerns about the war in Ukraine and whether victory is possible.

Victory Day, celebrated in Russia every year on May 9, marks the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in World War II.

The Kremlin dismissed reports in Western media that Mr Putin's protection has been intensified recently due to fears of a coup or assassination.

Russia has held its most scaled-back Victory Day parade in years due to fears of an attack by Ukraine, where victory for Moscow's forces still proves elusive after more than four years of fighting.

The parade, held every year on May 9 in Red Square, marks Russia's most revered national holiday — traditionally a time to celebrate the Soviet Union's World War II victory over Nazi Germany and to pay homage to the 27 million Soviet citizens who perished during the conflict.

Many of those citizens were from Ukraine, where Russia is now mired in the deadliest European conflict since World War II.

But despite fears that Ukraine would take the opportunity to strike the Russian capital, the parade went ahead peacefully, with Russian soldiers and sailors — some of whom had served in Ukraine — marching and cheering as President Vladimir Putin looked on.

Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a speech during Victory Day celebrations at Red Square. ( Kremlin.ru via Reuters )

The president, who was seated beside Russian veterans in the shadow of Vladimir Lenin's Mausoleum, later made an eight-minute speech promising victory in the war against Ukraine, which the Kremlin calls a "special military operation".

"The ⁠great feat of the victorious generation inspires the soldiers carrying out the tasks of the special military operation today," Mr Putin said.

Ukraine had earlier insisted it would not strike Red Square during Victory Day celebrations, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issuing a tongue-in-cheek decree "allowing" the May 9 military parade to go ahead.

Both Kyiv and the Kremlin also agreed to a three-day ceasefire stretching from Saturday to Monday, announced prior to Victory Day celebrations by US President Donald Trump.

The Australian embassy in Ukraine is on high alert after the Kremlin warned staff to evacuate ahead of possible "massive missile strikes" this weekend, as Moscow prepared to hold a scaled-down Victory Day parade.

Security, however, remained tight in Moscow, where soldiers with machine guns rode atop trucks and roads were blocked around the centre of the capital.

Russia had also warned that any attempt by Kyiv to disrupt Saturday's event would lead to a massive missile strike on the Ukrainian capital, with Moscow telling foreign diplomats they should evacuate Kyiv staff in the event of such an attack.

There was a palpable sense of relief in the Russian capital when no such attack eventuated.

"There were no strikes on the Red Square. Obviously, there was no ‌massive retaliatory missile strike on Kyiv from us," Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.

A Russian security officer stands guard ahead of Victory Day celebrations. ( Reuters: Anastasia Barashkova )

Ahead of the march, Russia and Ukraine each accused the other of violating unilateral ceasefires they had declared over recent ⁠days.

However, Donald Trump's announcement of a three-day ceasefire from Saturday to Monday , which also included an agreement for Russia and Ukraine to exchange 1,000 prisoners, appears to have held, with no breaches reported since.

Mr Trump spoke to reporters in Washington after announcing the deal, saying he would "like to see a big extension" of the ceasefire.

Ukrainians welcomed the three-day reprieve as a much-needed break from ​years of Russian attacks, even though the Kremlin said a longer-term peace deal remained a long way off.

The Ukrainian president called one attack in Poltava "especially vile", accusing Russia of launching a second missile while emergency rescuers were at the scene.

"On the one hand, this is very good because, honestly, the sleepless nights have gotten a bit tiresome," said Kateryna Kizev, a 22-year-old who ⁠fled the frontline city of Kherson in the south, and now lives in Cherkasy in central Ukraine.

"At ‌least for a few days we will be able to ​sleep in peace and without the attacks."

Kharkiv resident Ramaz Tsytsyashvili ‌said he hoped that the ceasefire would open the way for more talks to end the war.

"And perhaps there ​will be a miracle and this temporary silence, this ceasefire, will hold up a bit and continue, and then step by step it will move to negotiations, and affairs will be solved in offices, not on the battlefield," he added .

Women pay their respects to World War II dead at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Kyiv on Saturday. ( Reuters: Gleb Garanich )

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Moscow has pummelled power plants and other infrastructure across Ukraine with missiles and drones while Kyiv has attacked Russia's oil and gas production and export facilities.

Formal peace talks have stalled, with Ukraine rejecting Russia's demands that it surrender territory it has successfully defended since it pushed Russian ​forces ‌back from the capital early in the war.

"It is understandable that the American side is in a hurry," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told state television reporter Pavel Zarubin.

"But the issue of a Ukrainian settlement is far too complex, and reaching a peace agreement is a very long way ⁠with complex details."

Once used to show off Russia's vast military, including its nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missiles, this year's Victory Day parade had no tanks or other military equipment ‌rolling over the cobblestones of Red Square.

Instead, weapons including a Yars intercontinental ballistic missile, the new Arkhangelsk nuclear submarine, the Peresvet laser weapon, the Sukhoi Su-57 fighter, the S-500 surface-to-air missile system and a host of drones and artillery were shown on giant screens in Red Square and on state television.

North Korean troops, who fought against Ukrainians ‌in Russia's Kursk region, also marched, while Russian Su-25 fighters flew above the towers of the Kremlin.

Russian Su-25 jets release smoke in the colours of the Russian flag during Victory Day celebrations. ( Reuters: Ramil Sitdikov )

Russia holds its celebration of Nazi Germany's defeat on May 9 because the Germans' unconditional surrender came into force at 11:01pm on May 8, 1945, now marked as "Victory ‌in Europe Day" by Britain, the United States and France.

However, in Moscow it was already May 9, which became the Soviet Union's "Victory Day".

Ukraine, which was part of the Soviet Union until 1991 and lost millions in World War II, also celebrated Nazi Germany's defeat on May 9 up until Russia's 2022 invasion, when it moved its celebrations to May 8.

Some Ukrainians who lost relatives during World War II, however, still bring flowers to the Soviet soldiers' monuments on May 9.

This year's Victory Day parade took place amid a wave of anxiety in Moscow about the ultimate outcome of the ‌conflict in Ukraine.

The war has killed hundreds of thousands of ⁠people, left swathes of Ukraine in ruins and drained Russia's $US3 trillion ($4.1 trillion) economy, while Russia's relations with Europe are worse than at any time since the depths of the Cold War.

"The crisis is still deepening gradually, but any sharp movement can send the economy (and not only the economy) into a tailspin," said jailed pro-war Russian nationalist Igor Girkin on Telegram, who has criticised the Kremlin for its conduct of the war.

Girkin, a former Federal Security Service officer, used ⁠a naval analogy to say that Russia's leaders were more worried about being kicked out of their cabins than about a shipwreck.

Russian Defence Minister Andre Belousov took part in the parade. ( Kremlin.ru via Reuters )

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov this week dismissed reports from CNN and other Western media outlets that Mr Putin's protection had been intensified ‌because of fears of a coup ‌or assassination.

Other Russian officials also dismissed reports of a coup plot as nonsense.

CNN's reporting cited an unidentified European intelligence agency as saying that Mr Putin's former defence minister, Sergei Shoigu, was seen as a potential coup leader.

Mr Shoigu, Russia's Security Council secretary, attended an online meeting of the Security Council chaired by Mr Putin on Friday and was at the parade on Saturday, sitting beside some of Mr Putin's most powerful officials.

Reuters/ABC

Melbourne City progressed to the A-League Women's grand final with a 2-0 aggregate win over cross-town rivals Victory.

Shelby McMahon, 17, scored a stunning first-half goal to earn her side a 1-0 victory in the second leg in Melbourne.

City's opponent in next weekend's decider will be decided on Sunday, when Brisbane and Wellington face off in their second leg at Porirua Park.

A stunning strike from teenager Shelby McMahon has fired Melbourne City into the A-League Women's grand final, with her side notching a 1-0 win over cross-town rivals Victory in the second leg of their semifinal.

McMahon's match-winning moment came in the 34th minute at the City Football Academy, when she was alert to a bobbling ball on the edge of the penalty area and rifled home fiercely on the half-volley.

Despite plenty of attacking intent on either side of the 17-year-old's pinpoint finish, Victory was unable to find the goals needed to send the game into extra-time, with City advancing to the season decider with a 2-0 aggregate triumph.

Minor premiers City will play the winner of Sunday's other semifinal between Wellington and Brisbane at Melbourne's AAMI Park next Saturday.

The Roar carries a 2-1 lead over from the first leg at home into the second leg at Porirua Park.

Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Victory, who finished sixth on the ladder, had 56 per cent of the ball and the lion's share of the chances, with City goalkeeper Malena Mieres called into action on several occasions.

Kennedy White and Alana Jančevski were both denied by the City shot stopper in the first half, before the crossbar came to City's rescue late on.

"Overall, I thought we managed the game well," City coach Michael Matricciani told Paramount Plus and Network Ten.

"Our game plan worked, and we created our four or five chances as well.

"When Shelby puts that sort of goal away, it's a special moment."

Justin Longmuir has guided the Dockers to their second-best ever start to an AFL season. ( AAP Image/Richard Wainwright )

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir says he is having fun coaching the high-flying Dockers, after guiding them to eight-straight wins and into the AFL's top two.

The comments follow a throwaway line at Fremantle's season launch, when Longmuir declared there was no fun in his life.

His words were then revived in a cheeky banner by West Coast ahead of the Western Derby in April.

"There is plenty of fun in my life at the moment," Longmuir told ABC Perth's Sports Talk program on Saturday.

The Dockers stormed home to beat another premiership fancy in Hawthorn on Thursday night, booting the final five goals to win by 15 points.

Michael Frederick celebrates after kicking a goal during this week's match against the Hawks. ( AAP Image/Richard Wainwright )

A crowd of 54-thousand was at Perth Stadium, and was treated to Fremantle's famous "Wharfie Time", which sees the stadium's lights dim and the gong from AC/DC's Hells Bells rings out, lifting the crowd into a frenzy.

Longmuir says he cannot hear the sound from the coaches' box, but thinks it helps his side.

"I think it doesn't necessarily give our players a lift, because I think they're already getting a rise out of the crowd," he said.

"But I think it could spook the opposition, and some opposition players."

Fremantle played four games in 18 days, but now has a long break until next Sunday's clash with Essendon at Docklands.

The Dockers face Essendon next Sunday, before hosting St Kilda five days later. ( AAP Image/Richard Wainwright )

The Dockers then have a five-day turnaround before a huge home clash with St Kilda, which could set a new unbeaten streak record for the club if they win both upcoming matches.

Despite the tight fixtures, Longmuir is reluctant to rest players for the trip to Melbourne.

"We haven't really got a lot of sore players and we've been able to manage players really well throughout the week," he said.

"The five-day break is tricky, but we've also been able to manage players in-game as well with the five on the bench.

"Some of our players probably aren't playing as much game time as they would have played last year."

A notable absence from next Sunday's game will be captain Alex Pearce, who suffered a low-grade knee injury in the win over the Hawks and will miss at least a week.

"It's too early to say, but if it's not one, we're expecting it to be no more than sort of three matches," Longmuir said.

Fremantle captain Alex Pearce suffered a minor knee injury in the final minute of Thursday's win over the Hawks. ( AAP Image/Richard Wainwright )

"I know Alex has had his issues, and sometimes he's not the best one to go off an average game range.

"He's an important player to us, not only the way he plays — which is really proactive and physical — but also his leadership has been outstanding."

The Dockers' 8-1 start to the 2026 season is its best under Longmuir, bettering a 7-2 start in 2022.

The team's best-ever result was nine straight to open 2015.

The catchphrase "Flagmantle" was referenced heavily following the win over the Hawks, as the Dockers knocked off a difficult opponent to sit alongside Sydney at the top of the ladder.

But despite the outside noise, Longmuir was confident his side could handle the increased expectation.

Longmuir is confident his team is not being distracted by the growing media hype. ( ABC News: Kenith Png )

"Every time I bring it up that the lid might be off, and this and that, they don't really know," he said of his players' attitude to the hype around them.

"Modern-day footballers are not footy heads, so they're not reading footy content as much as players might have done in the past, which is holding us in good stead.

"It is an internal mantra of making sure we just win each day and be where our feet are.

"In the past, we've let ourselves down when we haven't valued the right things, or we haven't respected the opposition as much as we should have. And I think that speaks to our record last year.

Fremantle overcomes a 15-point deficit to beat Hawthorn thanks to a dominant final quarter.

"Our record last year against the best teams was really good. The best in the comp almost. But we let ourselves down against some teams we probably should have beaten, and that's through probably not respecting them or valuing the right things going into those games."

Despite the Dockers' lofty ladder position, Longmuir said there was still room for improvement.

"I said to the players after the game last week that we were going at about 85 per cent," he said.

"We're not going to play periods of the game all the time like we did in that last quarter. But those types of moments should be the cream on the top.

"Too often this year we've had quarters like the second quarter, where we've given the opposition a couple, we haven't quite made the most of our [opportunities] and all of a sudden it's a four-goal turnaround."
